analysis.one_liner: Lets consumer product safety regulators set safety standards for guns and gun parts.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 8 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bans the Consumer Product Safety Commission from regulating guns and gun parts as consumer products, so no federal agency sets safety standards for how firearms are designed. This bill would strike that ban, letting the Commission write rules the same way it does for cribs, toys, and power tools. The bill never got any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun buyers and their families, who would gain the same safety-recall and design-standards protections other consumer products have, and communities affected by accidental and unsafely designed firearms.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the legal exclusion that treats pistols, revolvers, and other firearms as outside the Consumer Product Safety Commission's jurisdiction, letting it issue safety standards for firearms and firearm components
Would apply the same regulatory framework used for other household products, which includes mandatory safety standards and recalls of defective items

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and component makers, who would face design and testing compliance costs and possible recalls; gun owners could see modestly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The Commission's authority could be used more aggressively than pure safety design; gun-rights opponents argue that allowing a safety agency to regulate firearm design could effectively restrict the availability or features of lawful firearms
Safety standards on gun design would address only part of firearm deaths; measures targeting access, storage, or illegal trafficking reach more of the problem
Manufacturers would bear compliance costs and recall exposure, which could be passed to buyers as higher prices

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: it adds design-safety and recall rules for a product category that is currently exempt, addressing accidental shootings and defective designs rather than overall gun violence. The main serious objection is that the same authority could be stretched into restrictions on lawful ownership, which is why the gun industry and gun-rights groups oppose any such jurisdiction. The compliance costs to manufacturers are real but comparable to what other product makers already face.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Cory Booker introduced the bill in the Senate on May 4, 2023, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors: Warren, Hirono, Menendez, Durbin, Feinstein, Reed, and Merkley
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced
No further action was taken for the rest of the Congress; the bill was never reported out of committee, never debated on the floor, and never received a vote

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers keep their long-standing exemption from consumer product safety regulation, and gun-rights groups avoid any precedent for federal safety oversight of gun design.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held, so it died at the end of the 118th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All eight cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; no vote was ever taken, so no formal roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from the Consumer Product Safety Act, exposing them to design standards, compliance costs, and recalls. Their interest in avoiding that oversight runs against the safety protections gun buyers would gain.

industries.industry: Firearms retailers and gun-rights advocacy groups
industries.note: Retailers would face altered product lines and possible recalls, and gun-rights organizations oppose any federal safety agency having jurisdiction over firearm design, arguing it could be used to restrict lawful ownership.
